title: Optimize walkthrough: prefetch + batch-sizing & cost model — Stratus Retail
summary: Redwood AE + SE ran an Optimize walkthrough focusing on KV/prefix prefetch strategy, batch sizing trade-offs, and a lightweight cost model for Stratus Retail's chat and product-recommendation workloads. Customer provided traffic shape and SLO constraints; team agreed to a sandbox pilot and deliver a tailored cost sim and security pack.
action_items: Maya Singh: Send tailored pricing + sample cost model by 2028-06-16
Ethan Cole: Provision sandbox and run 1-hour throughput sim (KV-prefetch scenarios) by 2028-06-18
Rahul Desai: Share 7-day production traffic heatmap and 95th percentile latency SLO by 2028-06-15
next_steps: Share security pack (SOC2 + KMS + VPC docs)
Run initial KV-prefetch hit-rate sensitivity sim and share spreadsheet
Follow-up call: results + pricing review (week of 2028-06-24)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-06-14 15:30 UTC
Duration: 49 minutes
Attendees: Maya Singh (Redwood AE), Ethan Cole (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Stratus - Dir ML), Rahul Desai (Stratus - Lead Backend), Tara Kim (Stratus - Head Infra)
Recording: https://redwood-recordings.example/ff-20280614-6782
Agenda: 1) Quick context/constraints; 2) Walkthrough Optimize recommendations (prefix/KV prefetch + batching); 3) Run a small cost model live; 4) Agree pilot and next steps.

Summary (auto): run-through of prefix vs KV prefetch, small live cost model plugged with Stratus sample numbers; agreed to sandbox pilot and deliverables.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Maya from Redwood, i'll kick us off. Ethan will do the deep parts. Hey Lena, Rahul, Tara, thanks for making time.
[00:12] Lena: yup thanks Maya, excited. we've been looking at your econ docs, trying to see where prefetch helps with our chatbot and product rec flows.
[00:18] Ethan: cool. quick clarifying q, the traffic you sent had two primary shapes? one chat-ish, avg seq ~280 tokens, and a short rec flow ~40 tokens?
[00:26] Rahul: yep that's right. chat is interactive, users send messages and often multi-turn, recs are basically short prompts for personalization. our 95th latency SLO is 350ms for recs, 1s for chat.
[00:36] Maya: perfect. so we'll focus two things: 1) prefix / KV prefetch strategies to reduce per-token cost on the multi-turn chat; 2) batching sizing heuristics so recs meet the tight 350ms SLO.
[00:46] Tara: and security wise we need VPC, KMS integration and audit logs, that was in the RFP.
[00:52] Ethan: noted. we'll surface that in the security pack. ok i'll share my screen — walking through Optimize -> Prefetch tab — apologies if the transcript gets weird on screen-share descriptions.
[01:15] [screen share noise] Ethan: on the left, there are prefetch policies, and here is our typical prefix cache policy — you can pin lifetime, eviction TTL and a max-kv-items per session. the idea is: cache the KV (key-value) attention cache after N tokens so subsequent turns short-circuit generation.
[01:38] Lena: wait, so how does prefix differ from a simple session cache? isn't prefix just caching the earlier tokens?
[01:44] Ethan: yeah, prefix cache stores the full token prefix with kvs. session cache is looser — it's more about session affinity and hot-keys. prefix is cheap for long-lived sessions where you get high locality; KV-prefetch is a proactive approach where we warm the KV cache for expected next prompts.
[02:05] Rahul: can you say more about warming? do you precompute multiple possible continuations?
[02:09] Ethan: good q. we don't fabricate continuations, instead we prefetch model KV states for typical continuation patterns — e.g., after system + user + few turns, we precompute the KV slices up to the prompt length likely to be re-used, so the decoder spends less time recomputing attention keys per request. it's a bit like lookahead caching.
[02:30] Maya: and the cost tradeoff is you pay GPU cycles to prefetch, which can blow up if you prefetch for too many user variants. so we recommend policy-based prefetching: only for sessions that are 'engaged' and exceed a threshold.
[02:46] [00:02:46 - minor crosstalk] Lena: what's a good threshold? 3 turns? 5?
[02:54] Ethan: for your traffic, with avg 280 tokens and 6.5 turns per engaged session, we suggested a threshold of 3 turns and prefetch up to 512 tokens of KV for the session-wide prefix for 65% of engaged sessions — that gave an estimated 40% token-cost reduction in our sim.
[03:18] Rahul: interesting — are these numbers from the generic model or tuned to our model sizes? we're using a 13B dense model with q4 quantization.
[03:26] Ethan: tuned. we plugged your model family and quantization into the cost sim; bigger models get more bang from prefetch because attention recompute is costlier. q4 reduces memory but compute remains.
[03:36] Tara: latency — if prefetch runs asynchronously, does it add latency to first request?
[03:41] Ethan: no, prefetch is async for subsequent requests; the first request will still pay the full cost. the benefit is on turn N+1+. For recs (short flows) prefetch isn't worthwhile because sessions are short; instead we recommend micro-batching and strict max batch latency.
[03:56] Maya: let's go to the cost model. I have a small spreadsheet where i'm plugging in your numbers — average tokens per request, traffic QPS, expected hit rate.
[04:05] [typing noises] Maya: ok plugging: chat QPS during peak is 22, avg session length 6.5 turns, avg tokens per turn 45 (gives ~292 tokens per session). recs QPS is 80, avg tokens 38.
[04:21] Maya: baseline (no prefetch, dynamic hosted) our sim shows X tokens billed per minute — sorry, there's a little transcription hiccup; i'm reading out numbers — baseline per-token compute cost estimate is $0.00045 / token for the 13B across our fleet with your region.
[04:42] Lena: that seems high compared to the docs? can you show where it's coming from?
[04:46] Ethan: it's the blended per-token with concurrency overhead on small sequences, also includes memory copy overhead on the accelerator for short requests. when we apply batching it drops a fair bit.
[04:55] [05:00] Maya: ok live sim: scenario A (no prefetch, optimize batching for recs): recs held to 300ms batch latency budget, target batch size 8 with max-wait 20ms, effective throughput meets SLO; cost per 1M recs = $720 (simulated).
[05:21] Maya: scenario B (chat + prefix prefetch): with a 65% prefix hit rate, we see chat token compute cost drop by ~38%, overall platform cost drop by ~24% for combined workload.
[05:34] Rahul: how sensitive is that to hit rate? if our hit rate is 40% instead of 65%?
[05:38] Ethan: good Q — we ran a hit-rate sweep: 40% hit -> savings ~22% chat cost, 65% -> 38%, 80% -> 46%. there's diminishing returns past ~75% because prefetch overhead increases marginally while hit improvements shrink for your traffic profile.
[05:58] Tara: what about concurrency? at 22 QPS chat, does prefetch require changing pool size?
[06:03] Ethan: it can — prefetch increases GPU occupancy. recommendation: carve a small dedicated pool for prefetch-warmed sessions (or use Dedicated with pinned capacity). For hosted we suggest a routing policy that favors your recs on low-latency nodes and routes warmed chats to high-throughput nodes.
[06:21] Maya: another option is session affinity routing — keep hot sessions on the same worker to raise the hit rate without prefetching every time, but that requires some sticky hashing in your front-end.
[06:33] Lena: sticky hashing might be hard with our autoscaler but doable at the edge. OK — security / compliance — Tara, any non-negotiables?
[06:42] Tara: KMS integration for model logs, VPC peering, and we need 12 mo audit logs for requests. SOC2 is required, and we asked about an on-prem package if needed.
[06:51] Ethan: all supported. Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and on-prem bundles. We'll include the SOC2 report, KMS integration doc and audit log retention options in the security pack.
[07:03] [07:03] Maya: i'm going to flip to the Console view — showing Optimize recommendations. you'll see a heatmap here that suggests the sweet spot for batch sizes vs max-wait latencies.
[07:15] Ethan: note the console's simulator accounts for KV cache warmup cost and amortizes it across expected hit windows. that model is configurable with your own heatmap data which you can upload.
[07:29] Rahul: we can export heatmap from our infra — should i send a csv with per-endpoint QPS / p95 / avg tokens?
[07:35] Maya: yes please, that fits perfectly. we'll ingest and rerun the sim.
[07:40] Lena: question on quantization — does q4 limit prefetch effectiveness?
[07:45] Ethan: q4 mainly affects memory layout; compute patterns are similar. prefetch still helps. if you move to int8 quant we might see performance differences; we'll flag that in the sim.
[07:58] [08:00] Maya: now quick demo of the sandbox run plan — we can provision a 24/7 sandbox for a week, ingest a sample of your traffic, and run three scenarios: baseline, prefix-prefetch, and sticky-session. we'll collect cost and p95 latency and surface a decision matrix.
[08:19] Rahul: how many GPUs would that need? we can allow a short-term quota increase.
[08:24] Ethan: for your peak shape, the sandbox with a 4-GPU A100-equivalent pool will let us run the sim at scaled QPS. it won't replicate full production concurrency but it's enough to validate hit rates and batch dynamics.
[08:38] Tara: any data residency concerns while in sandbox? we prefer EU-only hosts for the sample.
[08:43] Maya: we can spin the sandbox in eu-west region. note that if you need on-prem, the private package has a different provisioning timeline.
[08:52] Lena: could you share a simplified runbook for what metrics you'll capture?
[08:56] Ethan: yes — we'll capture QPS, avg latency, p95 latency, token consumption, GPU utilization, prefetch hit/miss, and per-request billed tokens.
[09:08] Maya: back to costs — i'll attach the spreadsheet after the call. quick sensitivity: if you increase hit rate 20 percentage points, ROI on prefetch shows payback in ~3 weeks of production traffic for a 4-GPU dedicated pool.
[09:22] Rahul: that payback calculation assumes immediate traffic stability; how do we account for burstiness?
[09:27] Ethan: we recommend burst capacity (2x) and autoscaling policies. also set fallback routes to a cheaper model variant if latency balloons. the Console can do automated fallback.
[09:39] [09:39] Maya: small aside — competitors often default to simple batching which can miss prefix-level savings. HydraCompute claims similar caching but it's proprietary and doesn't do the same smart routing we demoed.
[09:50] Lena: ok noted.
[09:53] Ethan: want to call out a failure mode: if prefetch warms for wrong user paths, you waste GPU cycles. so policy tuning and quick telemetry is essential — Optimize has built-in regression alerts tied to your eval sets.
[10:07] Tara: for the POC, what's the expected data we need to hand over?
[10:11] Maya: 1) traffic heatmap csv, 2) sample encrypted payloads (or synthetic equivalents) for privacy, 3) list of SLOs, 4) optional a small prompt set for eval quality checks.
[10:22] Rahul: we'll prepare those.
[10:25] [10:25] Maya: ok quick recap: Redwood to provision sandbox, run three scenarios, deliver a cost sim and a security pack; Stratus to share heatmap and SLOs; follow-up week of 6/24 to review results.
[10:40] Lena: sounds good. one more question on billing granularity — do you bill per-batched token served or per-inferred token including prefetch compute?
[10:48] Ethan: we bill per effective token — prefetch compute is included in the billed tokens for the sandbox sim but on enterprise contracts we can show an amortized line-item or negotiate reserved-seat pricing for prefetch-heavy workloads.
[10:59] Rahul: negotiable is good.
[11:02] Maya: ok action items we'll email. thanks everyone — do we want to set the follow-up for 30 minutes or 60?
[11:09] Lena: 30 should be enough to review sim summary.
[11:12] Maya: great. end notes: security pack, sandbox start ~6/19, follow-up 6/24 15:30 UTC. thanks all.
[11:20] [end recording]
